title: Fanout combiner timeout guardrails and customer escalation runbook
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Summary:
During repeated customer escalations (notably ACME Corp on 2025-02-12) we observed clusters of 5xx and timeout errors originating from the fanout/combiner layer in the hosted runtime. The combiner aggregates small, concurrent inference requests to reduce kernel invocation overhead. Under sudden tenant bursts the combiner was hitting an aggressive internal timer and cancelling gRPC streams upstream, which manifested as 502/504s and triggered SDK retries that amplified load.

Root cause hypothesis (multi-factor):
- Combiner timer configuration was optimized for steady-state batching (short windows). Under microburst patterns it frequently expired causing partial flush + cancel semantics.
- A recent kernel scheduling change (kernel scheduler v2) reduced effective headroom for short-sequence workloads, making the system more sensitive to microbursts.
- SDK retries (idempotency not universally used) produced retry amplification so cancelled requests were retried immediately, increasing pressure.

Impact:
- Multiple enterprise tenants experienced degraded availability and elevated 5xx rates for 10–30 minute bursts.
- Observable increase in token cost and customer frustration (support escalations, demo failures).

Proposed mitigation strategy (short and medium term):
1) Immediate mitigations (hotfix & runbook):
   - Increase combiner timeout from 5ms -> 20ms for the hosted fleet as an emergency, reducing flush/cancel churn. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3421)
   - Deploy a temporary tenant-level soft-shed: identify top 5 noisy tenants and reduce combiner weight for them via dynamic config.
   - Support instructs to enable SDK client-side exponential backoff and ensure idempotency tokens are used when possible. (SDK PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/987)
   - Update Pager steps and customer communication templates (Confluence runbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RE/Combiner+Timeout+Escalation).

2) Medium-term fixes (release in runtime-1.19):
   - Implement adaptive combiner window: combiner window adapts to observed arrival rate and sequence-length distribution. This reduces worst-case flush/cancel during bursts while preserving batching benefits at low load. (Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-adaptive-combiner)
   - Add a tenant-level token-bucket admission control in the routing layer to smooth bursts without global degradation.
   - Introduce graceful degradation path: when combiner detects overload it returns a fast fallback (cached prefix or 429 with Retry-After) instead of cancelling streams.

3) Long-term resiliency work:
   - Re-evaluate kernel scheduler v2 heuristics for short-sequence workloads; add telemetry to surface scheduler-induced headroom loss.
   - Expand per-tenant observability (burst heatmaps, queue latency P95/P99).

Trade-offs and risks:
- Increasing combiner window raises tail latency for single-request flows; we mitigate via adaptive windows.
- Tenant soft-shedding impacts noisy customers and must be coordinated with account teams.
- Adding admission control reduces peak throughput but improves overall system stability and SLO adherence.

acceptance_criteria: Adaptive combiner implemented and unit-tested in runtime-1.19
Canary rollout plan executed with automated rollback on >5% increase in 5xx or >10% increase in tail latency
Tenant admission control deployed and demonstrates reduced retry amplification in load tests
Customer-facing runbook and account comms templates published and linked to Support playbook
